chunks.text: 3 Method Based on x-ray, gaze, and language input, XGLASS learns f ⁡ ( P , G ) → y ^ f(P,G)\rightarrow\hat{y} , which processes a coronal CT intensity projection P P , enriched with a disease-specific gaze prior G G , in the form of an importance map. For clarity, the overall pipeline is illustrated in Figure 1 . Based on P P and G G , f f predicts a continuous importance vector y ^ \hat{y} of length Z target Z_{\text{target}} . Each entry of this vector represents the diagnostic relevance of a single axial slice with respect to the disease conditioned through the importance map. By learning f ⁡ ( P , G ) f(P,G) with a ViT-based regression model, we enable effective disease-specific sequencing of the CT volume, from which P P is obtained. In the following subsections, we first describe how to generate G G , then how to project a CT volume to obtain P P , and finally how we learn f f . 3.1 Disease-Conditioned Importance Maps A central component of XGLASS is the construction of disease-specific 2D importance maps G G that capture how expert radiologists navigate through chest X-rays. To obtain these priors, we leverage the eye-tracking data paired with dictated report texts, available in the REFLACX dataset [ 4 ] . For disease filtering for each report transcript, we use custom regular expressions similar to SARLE [ 11 ] to identify disease-specific mentions in the spoken text. The timestamps associated with these textual matches define a temporal window during which the radiologist was verbally describing the relevant findings. Prior work in psycholinguistics shows that speakers’ gaze reliably anticipates verbal articulation by more than one second, motivating the inclusion of a short pre-speech buffer on the order of 1–1.5 s [ 14 ] . Given the cognitive load and visual search demands of CT interpretation, we included a slightly longer pre-speech buffer of 2 s to ensure we capture all relevant fixation points.

Formally, the gaze pooling process is described as follows, for a spoken mention with start time t start t_{\mathrm{start}} and end time t end t_{\mathrm{end}} , we define the effective gaze window as [ t start − 2 ​ s , t end ] [t_{\mathrm{start}}-2\,\mathrm{s},\;t_{\mathrm{end}}] . All gaze fixations that fall into this window are then extracted, ensuring that only gaze from the relevant diagnostic moment contributes to the disease-conditioned importance map. To obtain a consistent spatial representation, we normalize each fixation with respect to the REFLACX chest bounding box ℬ chest = ( x 0 , y 0 , w , h ) \mathcal{B}_{\text{chest}}=(x_{0},y_{0},w,h) and discard fixations falling outside ℬ chest \mathcal{B}_{\text{chest}} (potentially resulting from tracker drift or blinks). The box-normalized coordinates are x ~ = x − x 0 w , y ~ = y − y 0 h , \tilde{x}=\frac{x-x_{0}}{w},\qquad\tilde{y}=\frac{y-y_{0}}{h}, so that ( x ~ , y ~ ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] 2 (\tilde{x},\tilde{y})\in[0,1]^{2} . We then aggregate the normalized fixations across studies for the same disease category and smooth them by placing a Gaussian at each fixation to obtain a continuous density map [ 43 ] . Since REFLACX contains frontal CXRs acquired in both AP and PA views, we additionally analyze whether the resulting gaze priors are sensitive to view-specific acquisition geometry. In Sec. B.3 of the supplementary material, AP- and PA-specific gaze maps show only minor differences in their superior–inferior profiles; therefore, we aggregate both views to maximize the number of gaze samples available per disease. The resulting disease-conditioned importance maps capture the aggregated spatial attention pattern for each finding and serve as weak expert annotation priors that are subsequently fused with coronal CT intensity projections to create the final input for XGLASS.

3.2 CT Volume Projection Our method takes two complementary sources of supervision: pre-computed, disease-specific 2D gaze importance maps derived from radiologist eye-tracking on chest X-rays using the REFLACX dataset [ 4 ] , and a volumetric CT dataset that shares matching disease findings and therefore ReXGroundingCT [ 3 ] is to our knowledge the largest CT dataset that fulfills our requirements. To project a given CT volume into the disease-conditioned importance map domain, we first need to perform an intensity projection followed by a projection window normalization. Intensity projection: CT volume projections enable us to project a given 3D volume into a 2D image, which in case of a coronal projection, is aligned with our disease-conditioned importance maps. Formally, let f ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) f(\mathbf{x}) denote the volumetric attenuation at location 𝐱 ∈ ℝ 3 \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} . A projection along an imaging direction 𝐝 \mathbf{d} samples parallel-beams 𝐱 ⁡ ( u , v , t ) = 𝐨 ⁡ ( u , v ) + t ​ 𝐝 \mathbf{x}(u,v,t)=\mathbf{o}(u,v)+t\,\mathbf{d} and applies an aggregation operator 𝒜 \mathcal{A} to the line signal f ⁡ ( 𝐱 ⁡ ( u , v , t ) ) f(\mathbf{x}(u,v,t)) : 𝒫 𝒜 ​ ( u , v ) = 𝒜 ⁡ ( { f ⁡ ( 𝐨 ⁡ ( u , v ) + t ​ 𝐝 ) } t ∈ [ 0 , L ] ) . \mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}(u,v)\;=\;\mathcal{A}\big(\{\,f(\mathbf{o}(u,v)+t\,\mathbf{d})\,\}_{t\in[0,L]}\big). (1) Because the coronal projection preserves the superior–inferior coordinate indexing axial slices, aggregating anterior–posterior depth retains the positional information required for axial slice selection. Accordingly, 𝐝 \mathbf{d} follows the anterior–posterior axis, while different choices of 𝒜 \mathcal{A} yield standard projection types.

To simulate real-world x-ray projection 𝒜 ℬ ​ ℒ \mathcal{A_{BL}} would resemble the Beer-Lambert law [ 36 ] , which assumes that x-rays are only attenuated but not reflected at 𝐱 \mathbf{x} : A BL ( u , v ) = exp ( − κ ∫ 0 L f ( 𝐨 ( u , v ) + t 𝐝 ) d t ) , \mathrm{A_{BL}}(u,v)\;=\;\exp(-\kappa\int_{0}^{L}f(\mathbf{o}(u,v)+t\,\mathbf{d})\,\mathrm{d}t), (2) whereby κ \kappa is the constant extinction coefficient, which models absorption and out-scattering. An average-intensity projection (AIP) in contrast uses the line integral normalized by its length: A IP ​ ( u , v ) = 1 L ​ ∫ 0 L f ⁡ ( 𝐨 ⁡ ( u , v ) + t ​ 𝐝 ) ​ 𝑑 t . \mathrm{A_{IP}}(u,v)\;=\;\frac{1}{L}\int_{0}^{L}f(\mathbf{o}(u,v)+t\,\mathbf{d})\,\mathrm{d}t. (3) In the field of radiology, additionally, the maximum-intensity projection (MIP), defined as A MIP ​ ( u , v ) = max t ∈ [ 0 , L ] ⁡ f ⁡ ( 𝐨 ⁡ ( u , v ) + t ​ 𝐝 ) \mathrm{A_{MIP}}(u,v)=\max_{t\in[0,L]}f(\mathbf{o}(u,v)+t\,\mathbf{d}) , plays an important role. However, MIPs emphasize very high-density structures (e.g. bones) and de-emphasize soft-tissue pathology, which conflicts with the intensity ranges in which our target findings occur. Therefore, throughout this paper, we solely focus on the Beer-Lambert projection and the AIP. We have ablated both (see Section 4.4.2 ), whereby we compare three standard CT windowings using AIP, i.e., lung, soft-tissue, and a wide window. Projection window normalization. To ensure the described intensity projections are aligned with the obtained disease-conditioned importance maps, anatomy normalization needs to be applied. During this normalization, our training set of 3,142 CT volumes was resampled to a uniform isotropic spacing of 1.25 × 1.25 × 1.25 1.25\times 1.25\times 1.25 mm. While this standardizes resolution, it does not reconcile variability in scan coverage along the Z Z -axis, which is critical since XGLASS 2D-to-3D matching expects a fixed amount of axial slices.

To avoid the anatomical distortion introduced by global resizing (i.e., stretching or squashing), we adopt a fixed-size cropping strategy and define a target axial block size Z target Z_{\text{target}} to be extracted from each volume. To further minimize exclusions, we sweep Z target Z_{\text{target}} to find an optimal setting. A CT volume V i V_{i} is included only if two constraints hold: (1) its total axial slice count Z total , i Z_{\text{total},i} (at 1.25 mm) is large enough to contain the block, and (2) its pre-computed chest bounding-box height Z bbox , i Z_{\text{bbox},i} (at 1.25 mm) fits within the block. V i ∈ Cohort final ⇔ ( Z total , i ≥ Z target ) ∧ ( Z bbox , i ≤ Z target ) V_{i}\in\mathrm{Cohort}_{\mathrm{final}}\;\Leftrightarrow\;\big(Z_{\text{total},i}\geq Z_{\text{target}}\big)\;\wedge\;\big(Z_{\text{bbox},i}\leq Z_{\text{target}}\big) We tested integer values Z target ∈ [ 128,512 ] Z_{\text{target}}\in[128,512] and found an optimal value of Z target = 240 Z_{\text{target}}=240 slices. This choice minimized exclusions by balancing chest-bbox inclusion (median Z bbox , i = 205 Z_{\text{bbox},i}=205 ) against total volume length (median Z total , i = 269 Z_{\text{total},i}=269 ). As a result, the final cohort comprises 2,078 unique CTs, with 1,064 excluded for not meeting the constraints. For all included CTs, we then extract a fixed axial block of 240 slices (1.25 mm spacing) centered on the chest bbox, yielding a standardized ReXGroundingCT subset with a consistent 240-slice axial size across scans. Further dataset statistics and category-selection details are provided in Sec. C of the supplementary material. Ground-truth slice-area vector extraction. A key advantage of XGLASS is that it does not necessarily require full 3D segmentation masks: it can also be trained using only the start and end slices of a finding, as demonstrated by the SE-Binary and SE-Smooth ablations in Sec. 4.4.1 .

When segmentation masks are available, as in ReXGroundingCT, we use the more detailed Slice-Area target by deriving per-slice relevance scores from the 3D ground-truth masks. Therefore each mask is converted into a 240-dimensional disease-area vector over the fixed axial block. Let A i A_{i} denote the disease area on slice i i , with A i = 0 A_{i}=0 when the finding is absent. We compute M = max j = 1 , … , 240 ⁡ A j , M=\max_{j=1,\dots,240}A_{j}, and define the target vector 𝐲 = ( y 1 , … , y 240 ) \mathbf{y}=(y_{1},\dots,y_{240}) by max-normalization: y i = { A i / M , if ​ M > 0 , 0 , if ​ M = 0 , i = 1 , … , 240 . y_{i}=\begin{cases}A_{i}/M,&\text{if }M>0,\\[4.0pt] 0,&\text{if }M=0,\end{cases}\qquad i=1,\dots,240. Thus, the slice with the largest disease extent receives y i = 1 y_{i}=1 , absent slices remain at 0 0 , and intermediate slices receive values proportional to their disease area. XGLASS reaches a relevant slice earlier and with lower variability than the baselines. 3.3 2D-3D Cross-Modal Slice Sequencing Our model builds on a ViT-B/16 backbone with AugReg ImageNet-21k pretraining [ 10 ] , which processes the fused representation of the disease-conditioned importance map G G and projected CT volume P P . To adapt the network from classification to slice-importance regression, we replace the original classification head with a lightweight two-layer MLP that outputs a fixed-length vector y ^ ∈ ℝ Z target \hat{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{Z_{\text{target}}} ( Z target = 240 Z_{\text{target}}=240 ). A final sigmoid activation constrains all predictions to the range [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , matching the normalized ground-truth slice–area profiles. The model receives a 3-channel 224 × 224 224\times 224 image initialized with a coronal CT intensity projection P P , replicated across all three input channels. The corresponding disease-specific importance map G G is then spatially scaled to the chest bounding-box region in the projection and blended into the red channel with an opacity coefficient α \alpha , while the green and blue channels remain unchanged. This channel-wise injection allows the ViT to process the anatomical projection and gaze-derived prior jointly in a single forward pass, enabling the model to estimate slice relevance directly from the fused representation. During training, the model obtains as input the fused G G and P P image, and learns to regress the ground-truth slice–area vector derived in Sec. 3.2 . For each input image, the network outputs y ^ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] 240 \hat{y}\in[0,1]^{240} and is optimized using MSE loss between y ^ \hat{y} and the corresponding normalized ground-truth vector y y .

We train the full model end-to-end using the AdamW optimizer with a differential learning rate schedule, assigning a higher learning rate to the regression head ( 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} ) and a lower rate to the ViT backbone ( 1 × 10 − 5 1\times 10^{-5} ). Training is performed with a batch size of 16. This setup preserves the pretrained backbone’s representational capacity while allowing the head to adapt to the slice-importance regression task. 4 Results We evaluate XGLASS on a held-out test set (split details in Supp. Sec. Let Z = 240 Z{=}240 be the number of axial slices, y ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] Z y\in[0,1]^{Z} the ground-truth slice-area vector, and y ^ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] Z \hat{y}\in[0,1]^{Z} the predicted importance scores and a slice is positive if y i > 0 y_{i}>0 . Unless otherwise noted, all metrics are computed per study and then macro-averaged. For overall ordering quality, we use ROC-AUC and Spearman’s rank correlation ρ \rho [ 34 ] between y y and y ^ \hat{y} over all Z Z slices, which directly evaluates agreement of the complete 240-slice ordering from most to least relevant. For practical analysis of performance on downstream tasks, we measure the hit rate at K K (Hit@ K K ) by sorting slices in descending y ^ \hat{y} and checking whether any positive slice appears among the first K K predicted slices. Further, we also calculate the average recall at K K (AR@ K K ), indicating the fraction of all GT positive slices that are represented within the K K predictions. In summary, higher ρ \rho and ROC-AUC indicate better global ranking alignment, higher Hit@ K K shows that a GT slice is in the K K predictions, and AR@ K K reflects the percentage amount of all GT slices inside K K predictions. 4.2 Baselines We benchmark XGLASS against the state-of-the-art slice selection method Vote-MI [ 41 ] , a BioMedCLIP-based slice-wise retrieval baseline [ 47 ] , heuristic and prior-only baselines, two 3D-native baselines [ 6 , 9 ] , and a gaze-free variant of our model. Only the gaze-prior baseline and gaze-guided XGLASS use REFLACX gaze information; BioMedCLIP, 3D Merlin + MLP, 3D U-Net, and XGLASS are disease-conditioned, while XGLASS (w/out gaze), Vote-MI, Gaussian Centered, and Random are disease-agnostic. Gaze prior only ranks slices using only the disease-specific gaze-derived superior–inferior profile, without patient-specific CT input, serving as a control for static anatomical prior effects.

Vote-MI was originally proposed for brain MRI; we follow its preprocessing and two-stage slice-selection procedure, but adapt it to thoracic CT by replacing the original feature extractor with MedVAE [ 40 ] , a medical foundation model, and convert the selected representatives into continuous slice scores for fair metric-based comparison. BioMedCLIP is used as a slice-wise image–text retrieval baseline. For each CT-condition pair, we encode all axial slices with the BioMedCLIP image encoder and the queried disease text with the text encoder, and then rank slices by image–text cosine similarity to obtain a disease-conditioned 240-dimensional relevance score vector. Full prompt and implementation details are provided in Supplementary Sec. G.1 . For the 3D-native model comparisons, 3D Merlin + MLP uses a frozen Merlin volumetric encoder [ 6 ] followed by a disease-conditioned MLP trained to regress the same 240-dimensional slice-relevance target as XGLASS, ands 3D U-Net [ 9 ] uses a 3D U-Net encoder trained from scratch on ReXGroundingCT with a slice-regression head for the same targets. Further implementation details for both 3D baselines are provided in Supplementary Sec. G.2 . XGLASS (w/o gaze cues) uses the identical backbone, projections, loss, and training as XGLASS but disables the gaze blend ( α = 0 \alpha{=}0 ), isolating the architecture without disease-specific importance priors. Gaussian Centered places a Gaussian bump over slice indices with fractional width σ frac \sigma_{\text{frac}} , yielding higher scores near the mid-thorax, and Random draws an independent score for each slice from Uniform ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] \mathrm{Uniform}[0,1] to reflect chance performance. All methods output a 240-dimensional score vector per study and are evaluated with the same metrics (ROC-AUC, Spearman’s ρ \rho , Hit@K, and AR@K), as described in Section 4.1 . G.4 . 4.3 Overall Performance Table 1 shows that gaze-guided XGLASS outperforms the 2D baselines across all reported metrics, with paired bootstrap intervals indicating significant gains in Hit@5, Hit@10, AUC, and Spearman’s ρ \rho . The native 3D baselines are competitive on global ranking metrics, with 3D U-Net achieving the highest AUC and Spearman’s ρ \rho point estimates and 3D Merlin achieving the highest Hit@1 and AR@10 point estimates. Despite operating on the full CT volume, the 3D baselines do not translate their small non-significant advantages in Hit@1 and global ranking into reliable slice retrieval and XGLASS remains significantly better on Hit@5 and Hit@10, the most relevant metrics for prioritizing a compact inspection set. Figure 3 further shows that XGLASS reaches the first diagnostically relevant slice earlier and more consistently than all baselines. In the coverage analysis (Figure 3 ), the 3D baselines become competitive, but together with their later first-hit distributions in Figure 3 , it suggests that the 3D models recover dense relevant regions once the correct location is found, but are less reliable at finding that location in every case. A case-level Miss@10 analysis supports this interpretation: Merlin and 3D U-Net miss the early inspection budget in 190/316 and 202/316 cases, respectively, compared with only 138/316 missed cases for XGLASS, indicating that their slightly higher Hit@1, AR@10, and global-ranking point estimates do not translate into more reliable compact-budget retrieval.

For clinical use cases, reliably surfacing at least one diagnostic slice within the inspected budget is more valuable than dense coverage only after successful localization, making XGLASS more suitable for practical slice selection, especially since it also requires 34.8 × \times less inference time and 6.5 × \times less GPU memory than Merlin, and 130.8 × \times less time and 10.9 × \times less memory than U-Net. 4.3.1 Disease-specific Performance The per-category trends in Table 2 align with typical anatomical distributions. Consolidation and Pleural abnormalities are often gravity-dependent and cluster in posterior lower lobes, producing a relatively narrow and predictable band along the z z -axis. This yields the highest AUC/ ρ \rho and strong Hit@K performance. Ground-glass opacities are frequently diffuse and extend across adjacent slices, which lifts mid- to higher- K K retrieval (e.g., Hit@10) but softens global ranking metrics. In contrast, lung nodules/masses are small, sparse, and spatially unpredictable along the z z -axis, which reduces the chance that the very top-ranked slices contain a hit and depresses global rank agreement. Thus, lung nodules are relatively less suited to our approach due to their small size and variable location, characteristics that also make them challenging for slice-selection methods in general. When evaluated only on the lung-nodule subset, XGLASS achieves the strongest Hit@K and AUC, showing that despite performing worse than on other diseases, it still provides the best slice prioritization (Supplementary Sec. D ). Taken together, these findings indicate that XGLASS learns disease-specific z z -axis priors similar to radiologist behaviour, prioritizes anatomically informative regions, and therefore performs best for conditions with consistent spatial distributions such as consolidations. 4.3.2 Computational Efficiency XGLASS contains approximately 86M parameters and is trained on a single 2D projection per CT study.

On an NVIDIA RTX 4080, one training epoch over 2,512 projections with batch size 16 takes 62.2 s, corresponding to roughly 40 samples/s, with approximately 3 GB peak GPU memory. Early stopping on validation loss consistently selects checkpoints after 6–8 epochs, yielding a complete training run in under 10 minutes. At inference time, XGLASS processes a full CT study, including intensity projection, in approximately 0.025 s per finding (0.150 s for all findings) with an estimated cost of 33.7 GFLOPs and 0.34 GB memory. In comparison, Vote-MI requires 7.51 s and approximately 116.33 TFLOPs per CT, while slice-wise BioMedCLIP requires 1.40 s and approximately 8.09 TFLOPs per CT. The 3D Merlin and U-Net baselines require 0.87 s and 3.27 s per finding, respectively, with 2.21 GB and 3.72 GB peak inference memory, making them 34.8 × \times /130.8 × \times slower and 6.5 × \times /10.9 × \times more memory-intensive than XGLASS. Overall, XGLASS is orders of magnitude cheaper than slice-wise 2D baselines and substantially faster and more memory-efficient than the 3D baselines, making local retraining on commodity GPUs feasible for institutions with private clinical data. 4.3.3 Downstream Slice-wise VLM Screening We evaluate XGLASS as a disease-conditioned pre-filter for slice-wise VLM screening with 2D VLMs. For each CT-condition pair, XGLASS ranks all axial slices by relevance to the queried finding, and the downstream model is evaluated only on the Top- K K selected slices. Metrics are computed over the inspected slices and compared against applying the same model to all 240 slices. Prompts, detailed inference settings and a matched-budget comparison to other slice selection methods are provided in Supplementary Sec. G . As shown in Fig. 4 , smaller XGLASS budgets consistently improve precision across MedGemma 4B [ 35 ] , Lingshu 7B [ 44 ] , and BioMedCLIP [ 47 ] , indicating that XGLASS determines disease-enriched slice subsets.

This also improves F1 over inspected slices at small budgets: Top-30 improves F1 from 0.288 to 0.414 for MedGemma, from 0.327 to 0.441 for Lingshu, and from 0.235 to 0.316 for BioMedCLIP. Compared with other slice-selected subsets, XGLASS improves average Top-30 F1 over the strongest 2D selector from 0.338 to 0.390, while remaining competitive to the strongest 3D selector. Evaluating fewer slices also reduces downstream runtime, with Top-30 requiring only 12.5% of the slice-wise model calls compared with all-slice inference. This supports XGLASS as a fast pre-selection step that enriches disease-relevant slices before costly slice-wise VLM review, 2D dataset curation or similar applications. 4.4 Ablation Studies We perform targeted ablations to isolate the effect of the main XGLASS design choices. Hyperparameter choices were made using the validation split resulting in ViT-B/16 backbone, AIP-wide CT projection, gaze blending strength of α = 0.75 \alpha{=}0.75 , and training using MSE. The corresponding validation results and selection criteria are reported in Supplementary Sec. E . All ablations tables modify only one factor at a time, and are reported on the held-out test set. Additional backbone, multi-channel-fusion, gaze-prior perturbations, loss ablation, and gaze prior-specificity ablations are provided in Supplementary Sec. F . 4.4.1 Weak Supervision. Our best training target uses segmentation-derived slice-area scores, but XGLASS can also be trained from substantially weaker annotations. We evaluate three reduced-supervision targets: SE-Binary , which marks all slices between annotated start and end positions as positive; SE-Smooth , which additionally applies Gaussian smoothing to this interval; and Rel-Rank , which uses relative slice ranking instead of dense area scores. As shown in Table 3 , reduced-supervision targets remain competitive, highlighting XGLASS’s ability to be trained from weak annotations. Table 3 : Supervision Target Ablation.

XGLASS significantly improves Hit@5 and Hit@10 over the strongest evaluated 2D and 3D baselines while remaining computationally efficient. Downstream experiments further show that XGLASS enriches compact disease-relevant candidate sets, improves downstream classification performance, and reduces slice-wise model calls. Beyond slice selection, XGLASS illustrates how heterogeneous 2D supervision can help bridge the gap between 2D foundation models and 3D medical image analysis. Nevertheless, several limitations remain. Despite surveying publicly available CT datasets, ReXGroundingCT is the only dataset, that overlaps with the 14 REFLACX-derived disease priors, yielding only to one dataset and six shared thoracic findings for evaluation. Our downstream screening experiments provide an initial demonstration of XGLASS utility and not direct use cases; broader applications such as VQA, report generation, retrieval, and localization remain future work. Appendix C CT Dataset and Volume Projections C.1 Dataset Selection To evaluate how effectively our disease-specific eye-tracking priors transfer from CXR to CT, we require a CT dataset that (i) provides report text and findings aligned with individual volumes, and (ii) contains findings that can be reliably matched to our REFLACX-derived disease-specific importance maps. As discussed in Section 3.2 , ReXGroundingCT [ 3 ] is, to our knowledge, the only large-scale CT dataset that satisfies both criteria. Because this dataset will also be used to train XGLASS, each disease category must be supported by a sufficient number of CT studies. We therefore exclude any finding category with fewer than 100 matching CTs. As shown in Figure 7 and Figure 8 , only six of the 14 REFLACX-defined categories reach this threshold in our standardized 240-slice ReXGroundingCT subset introduced in Section 3.2 , and we consequently restrict our experiments to these six categories. C.2 Training Dataset and Splits We use an 80/10/10 CT-volume-level train–validation–test split of the standardized 240-slice ReXGroundingCT subset, with no volume overlap between partitions and all findings from each CT retained in the same split.

This yields 2,514/306/316 CT–finding cases for training/validation/testing, respectively, totaling 3,136 cases across six categories: Lung nodule or mass (1,096), Groundglass opacity (925), Atelectasis (412), High lung volume (301), Consolidation (284), and Pleural abnormality (118), as shown in Fig. 8 . The disease distribution in our ReXGroundingCT subset is markedly imbalanced across our six categories. However the best performing model did not apply class-balancing or reweighting (e.g., oversampling, inverse-frequency sampling, focal/weighted losses), because the most prevalent class, lung nodule or mass , is also the hardest to localize due to its small size, variable location, and sparse slice extent. This choice is supported by the disease-specific results in Table 2 of the main paper, where XGLASS improves across all disease categories, and by the loss-function ablation in Sec. F.5 , where reweighted objectives do not improve small-finding and overall retrieval performance. Figure 9 : CT volume projections in XGLASS. C.3 CT Volume Projections For XGLASS, each 3D chest CT volume is converted into a 2D coronal intensity projection that lives in the same domain as our disease-conditioned importance maps, as explained in Section 3.2. Formally, we project along the anterior–posterior axis and aggregate attenuation values along each ray using an operator A A (Beer–Lambert or average-intensity), yielding a coronal image P A ​ ( u , v ) P_{A}(u,v) for each volume.

In the main experiments we focus on two projection families: (i) a physically motivated Beer-Lambert projection that mimics x-ray transmission, and (ii) average-intensity projections (AIP) combined with standard CT windowings. For AIP we consider three clinical window settings: a lung window, a soft-tissue window, and a wide window spanning a broad Hounsfield range. As discussed in Section 3.2 and ablated in Section 4.4.2, Beer-Lambert provides slightly better global ranking (AUC, Spearman), whereas AIP with a wide window offers the best early retrieval utility (Hit@K). Figure 9 illustrates how a single CT scan appears under these different projection choices, highlighting how windowing and projection type emphasize complementary structures (e.g., parenchyma in the lung window vs. mediastinum and pleural surfaces under broader windows). C.4 Gaze-Prior Blending Strength In XGLASS, the 2D CT projection and the disease-specific REFLACX gaze importance map are combined by injecting the normalized gaze heatmap H d ​ ( u , v ) H_{d}(u,v) into the red channel inside the chest bounding box using a blending coefficient α ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \alpha\in[0,1] . Here, α = 0 \alpha=0 corresponds to the CT-only input, whereas larger values increase the contribution of the disease-conditioned gaze prior in the fused representation. Figure 11 illustrates the qualitative effect of varying α \alpha for representative CT studies. The quantitative test-set ablation of α \alpha is reported in Sec. 4.4.3 of the main paper. The final value α = 0.75 \alpha{=}0.75 was selected on the validation split, as described in Sec. E . First, we evaluate the CXR gaze prior alone by averaging each disease-specific gaze map along the left–right axis, interpolating the resulting superior–inferior profile to 240 axial positions, and ranking slices by profile intensity. Second, we construct an empirical CT location prior using only train+val labels by averaging slice-presence vectors for each disease category and applying the resulting fixed category-specific prior to all corresponding test cases.

Third, we replace the gaze map in XGLASS with this CT-derived prior converted into a synthetic heatmap and fuse it with the CT projection in the same way as the gaze heatmap. Since this CT prior is computed from train+val ground-truth slice-presence targets from the same CT dataset distribution, it represents an empirical average lesion-location prior for each abnormality. In contrast, the gaze prior is transferred from CXR eye-tracking and does not use CT lesion-location statistics; instead, it captures radiologist visual search patterns that include both observed abnormality regions and plausible candidate regions inspected for each finding. In contrast, the CT-derived prior is less reliable when abnormalities occur in rare locations, whereas the broader radiologist search patterns encoded by the gaze prior can still overlap these regions, supporting the use of gaze over CT derived location priors. Table 10 shows that CT location statistics are informative: the CT location prior alone achieves the best Hit@1 and Spearman correlation. However, the full gaze-guided XGLASS model achieves the best AUC and performs substantially better for utility-centric top- K K retrieval metrics, improving Hit@10 from 0.453 0.453 to 0.563 0.563 and Hit@20 from 0.522 0.522 to 0.693 0.693 compared with the CT location prior alone. Injecting the CT-derived prior into XGLASS also improves over CT-only input at Hit@10 ( 0.535 0.535 vs. 0.468 0.468 ). Nevertheless, gaze-guided XGLASS remains stronger at Hit@10 and Hit@20, indicating that the transferred radiologist gaze prior provides complementary information beyond average CT lesion-frequency statistics, which improves the slice selection performance especially for higher K K . We additionally stratify test samples by their typicality under the train+val CT location prior, defined as the average CT-prior score over the ground-truth positive slices of each test sample.

In low-typicality cases, where the empirical CT prior assigns low probability to the true lesion region, the CT location prior drops sharply to Hit@10 of 0.151 0.151 . In contrast, the CXR gaze prior alone remains stronger at Hit@10 of 0.330 0.330 , while full XGLASS reaches Hit@10 of 0.358 0.358 and Hit@20 of 0.528 0.528 . This suggests that empirical CT priors primarily capture common dataset-specific lesion locations, whereas radiologist gaze priors cover broader disease-specific search regions. Combined with patient-specific CT projection evidence, this leads to more robust disease-conditioned slice prioritization than static location priors alone.
